Yesterday I talked to a like-minded (childfree) person. It was horrifying.

This woman (35) has known all her life that she doesn't want children. Her boyfriend of 14 years does. Well, at least one. She has decided to cave and give him the kid he wants, some time soon. When I asked why, she replied "what am I gonna do, throw away a relationship of 14 years?"

This woman is a great person and I love to have her in my life, but this is something I just cannot comprehend. This has written "sunk cost fallacy" all over it. I think there's a very high chance that she will end up very, very unhappy. It saddens me so much.

Maybe I should be grateful every day that I will never, under any circumstances, budge on being childfree. I will never enter a long-term relationship with a woman who wants a child in the long run, that's a certainty to me. Damn, I'm so glad to live in a country where more and more people decide to be childfree, otherwise I'd probably be single for life.
"I have to give him a kid, what else am I supposed to do?"

I know what I would do (NOPE), but I can understand the challenge this woman faces. What I'm astounded at is the 14 years together. It really depends on your friend and how direct you can be, the reasons why she is childfree and her outlook on life.

Perhaps you can present her with the idea of her child when they are grown up, learning that she did not want children, and how that would make the son/daughter feel - to be brought into the world while not truly being wanted.

You could play into her fears and talk about how, despite the fact that nobody wants to raise a bad person, bad people exist. Even with the best intentions and love, raising kids can go wrong... so how wrong can it go when the child is not wanted? Is she even sure she can love unconditionally? Could she love a sociopath? Could she love even when her child is testing her to her limits, intentionally?

You could bring up the fact that motherhood changes people. Not just friend circles, habits, lifestyle... but acute psychological, emotional and bodily changes that are irreversible. She'd never feel the same way again, physically. If she's proud of her body now, she will likely never be able to reclaim it. If she's unhappy with her body now, she's at the top of a slippery slope and it will only go downhill.

Ask her what if she got twins, triplets, or more (there is roughly a 3% chance to have more than one baby, which is huge... especially if her boyfriend only expects one child). What if she had a disabled child? Do they have the time and the financial stability for that? What if she had a miscarriage? She's delving into the unknown and there's no way to prepare for that. There are some things you just can't mitigate, and she will sturggle with these things more than most mothers because she does not want to be a mother in the first place.

Ask her if her boyfriend has any real plans for child-rearing. Not the fun stuff, but everyday nitty gritty things like feeding, changing, bathtimes, dropping them off at school, bla bla. It's likely that he hasn't really considered it, and the responsibilities will come to her.

Ask her to consider that her relationship with her boyfriend would be changed by a child. It would no longer be the same relationship that she had spent 14 years forging. No time together, no sleep, no privacy, no peace... stressful life.

You could ask her what if, after she gave her boyfriend a child, he left her. Of course nobody expects this, but it's plausible and she can just imagine it. That's a true horror story. She'd still have lost her relationship of 14 years, and now she'd have a bleak future as a single mom.

There might not be an angle to get through to her, but you can say you tried. I'd personally say screw the boundaries. This is the lives of several people we're talking about, not just her own. If she does decide to acquiesce to her partner's wishes, she might realise you were right (too late, I know that doesn't help) and thank you for it, and appreciate your friendship. Alternatively, she might just handle motherhood and grow to enjoy it, then there is nothing lost. Who knows. I'm sorry I can't be of more help.

I wrote this for Reddit's Childfree FAQ a while ago, and I've not encountered anything to disprove it.

Q: I do not want kids, but my SO does. What can I say or do to change her/his mind?

A: Nothing more than could be said to you to get you to change your mind. If you've talked it over and both decide through thoughtful deliberation that you still stand on opposing sides of potential parenthood, your relationship has three possible outcomes:

  1. You will acquiesce to the wishes of your partner and have a child. You will likely become bitter and miserable, and your child will suffer for it, even with your best intentions.
  2. Your partner will acquiesce to your wishes, and may very well become bitter and resentful toward you.
  3. You will both realize your life goals are incompatible and part.

Your young child is all of the sudden 6 months again. Dad's, what would you do differently?

Even more hiking.
I was fortunate to be able to hike regularly with my babies - Bjorn, FTW - and breathe in their little wispy hairs as we worked up a sweat together. I'd pull over to trees so they could feel different kinds of bark. We'd park ourselves creekside to see, smell, and feel the things we found there. If it were possible to OD on fresh air, that was the goal. My kids scrambled up boulders a year before they could walk.

Still - - I know we could have done more. Especially with my second child (as many of you probably already know, child two = way more than twice the effort). I could have made it work with the two children if I'd juggled my efforts with the jogging stroller more efficiently.

It is good for you, it is good for them. Depending on spacing - a second child is going to be hand delivered a shit-ton more illness than your first b/c the first is in school earlier. Everybody is going to be sick. It's going to seem like this lasts for years - because it sort of does. Get outside together. There is no better way to start, IMO.
